full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Recognize Schedule VI as a Massachusetts prescription-drug classification rather than a federal controlled schedule.
Apply Massachusetts prescription elements, oral documentation, electronic-prescribing exceptions, and transfer rules without inventing federal consequences.
Apply the Schedule VI validity clock and the additional-drug consequences instead of treating Schedule VI as a consequence-free label.
Recognise that the Schedule VI classification carries its own scope-of-practice consequence for who may transfer a prescription.

quick_review.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.
Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, while all other validity requirements remain applicable.
An oral controlled-substance prescription must be reduced to writing immediately with the required information; the separate duty to deliver a later follow-up prescription does not reach Schedule VI.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug becomes reportable to the prescription monitoring program and requires a customer identifier at dispensing.
Schedule VI is the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform a prescription transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized; the federal one-time transfer limit does not reach it, because Schedule VI is not a federal schedule.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I-V.
decision_logic.action: Classify it under Schedule VI, then identify the separate rule governing validity, documentation, dispensing, or transfer.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is written or oral rather than electronic.
decision_logic.action: Do not reject it solely for that format; apply the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception and all remaining prescription requirements, including the form requirements that still govern a written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A patient requests transfer of a Schedule VI prescription with authorized refills remaining.
decision_logic.action: Use the remaining-refill transfer pathway under 247 CMR 9.14(4): the prescription may move up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, that regulation bars transfer more than one year after issue, and a certified pharmacy technician may carry out the transfer with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is presented more than one year after its issue date, or with no refills remaining and the prescriber cannot be reached in time.
decision_logic.action: Do not refill it; consider only the professional-judgment continuation of a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI medication being dispensed has been designated an additional drug by the Department.
decision_logic.action: Obtain a customer identifier and treat the dispensing as reportable, using the documented hardship route only on its own terms.

ma_vs_federal.text: Schedule VI is a Massachusetts classification and does not itself make a drug federally controlled.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug carries Massachusetts prescription-monitoring and customer-identifier duties that the Schedule VI label alone does not imply.

exceptions.text: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes that format mandate, not the required prescription elements or oral documentation duties.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may in professional judgment dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), and from 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) as well, so the Schedule VI validity clock, the day-counting convention and the customer-identifier duty all fall away for that facility type.
In deciding whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after it was written as day one, so the Schedule VI one-year period does not include the issue date itself.

The follow-up duty Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's obligation to deliver an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception.

The Failover is a Schedule VI device: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up, provided its three conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the regulatory one-year limit.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: 1 year from the date of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: A licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year.

timing_deadlines.event: Transmission of prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing
timing_deadlines.timeframe: By the end of the next business day
timing_deadlines.consequence: Each transmission carries every controlled substance dispensed since the previous one.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist must immediately reduce an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing with the required Massachusetts prescription information.
A customer identifier must be obtained when dispensing a Schedule VI additional drug; the hardship route requires a documented reason and the recipient's printed and signed name and address.

A written Schedule VI prescription must carry the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

The elements a Massachusetts controlled-substance prescription must state are the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the date, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the substance, the patient's name and address except on a veterinary prescription, the directions for use with any required cautionary statements, and the number of times it may be refilled.

role_duties.duty: Validate required prescription elements even when the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception applies.
Check the Schedule VI validity clock and any additional-drug designation before dispensing rather than treating Schedule VI as consequence-free.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as an exemption from all prescription validity requirements is incorrect.
Treating Schedule VI as a federal schedule creates legal consequences that the Massachusetts classification does not supply.

The one-year rule in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) governs transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills and is separate from the one-year prescription validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12); neither should be restated as the other.
Concluding that Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program duties overlooks Schedule VI drugs designated as additional drugs.
Generalising the certified-technician transfer authority beyond Schedule VI ignores the word only in the regulation.
Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as removing every format requirement leaves the pharmacist filling a written prescription that no permitted format supports.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V; Schedule VI status does not itself make a drug federally controlled or routinely MassPAT-reportable.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts requirements for dispensing and refilling prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for ONE YEAR from the date of issue and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year. If a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner, the pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity NOT TO EXCEED 14 DAYS or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. Under 247 CMR 9.04(15) the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(12) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
exceptions: 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12).
The continuation supply is a professional-judgment allowance conditioned on inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization; it is not an automatic refill.

authority.name: Standards for prescription format and security in Massachusetts
DCP Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts generally requires covered prescriptions to be issued electronically subject to 105 CMR 721.070 exceptions and waivers. Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the state electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). Under 105 CMR 721.070(C), a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that the prescription properly falls within an electronic-prescribing exception or waiver; all other prescription and controlled-substance requirements still apply.
exceptions: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9).
Other enumerated exceptions and waivers may permit a covered prescription to be issued in written or oral form.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: On receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance, the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information required by M.G.L. c. 94C §20 and make a reasonable effort to authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber; the subsection requiring later electronic or written documentation expressly does not apply to Schedule VI.
exceptions: The follow-up prescription requirement in §20(c) does not apply to Schedule VI, but immediate reduction to writing and validity duties still apply.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A controlled-substance prescription must include the practitioner, patient, drug, strength, directions, date, registration, cautionary, and refill information required by Massachusetts law.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Certified pharmacy technician Schedule VI transfer scope

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under current 247 CMR 9.14, a pharmacy must timely transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or authorized agent, may act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer, and may not charge a transfer fee. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions; remaining authorized refills may be transferred, but a Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issuance. Under 247 CMR 8.04, a certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with approval of the pharmacist on duty.
exceptions: Schedule-specific federal requirements may add restrictions for federally controlled prescriptions; do not automatically import those mechanics into a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The Commissioner MAY DETERMINE that a drug is an 'additional drug' for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012 because it carries a BONA FIDE POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, based on factors including a risk of addiction alone or with a Schedule II through IV drug, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, or a known contribution to overdose or regular presence in the bloodstream of persons who have overdosed. UPON MAKING SUCH A DETERMINATION THE COMMISSIONER SHALL NOTIFY ALL DISPENSERS THAT THEY MUST BEGIN TO REPORT the dispensing of that additional drug pursuant to prescription as directed in 105 CMR 700.012(A).

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A licensee shall require a CUSTOMER IDENTIFIER, being the identification number on a valid government issued identification obtained by inspecting the identification of the ultimate user or their agent, on dispensing a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). A licensee may dispense WITHOUT one only if it has reason to believe that refusing would cause SERIOUS HARDSHIP to the ultimate user or agent AND DOCUMENTS THE REASON, AND the recipient PRINTS name and address on the reverse of the prescription or in a prescription log AND SIGNS it. The Commissioner may waive or modify the requirement for refills, deliveries or other specified activities.
exceptions: Documented serious hardship with the recipient's printed name, address and signature
Commissioner waiver or modification for refills, deliveries or other specified activities

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In order to determine whether a prescription is WITHIN DATE, a pharmacist shall count the DAY AFTER the prescription was written as DAY ONE. The issue date itself is not counted, so a period measured in days runs from the following day.

authority.name: Commissioner exceptions permitting written and oral prescriptions
Follow-up documentation for an oral prescription issued under an ePrescribing exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription shall cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS; if the practitioner has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), the practitioner shall instead cause a WRITTEN prescription to be delivered within not more than 7 DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law, postmarked within that period. The follow-up prescription must indicate that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it reduced to writing. Under 105 CMR 721.070(B) a practitioner issuing an oral prescription for a controlled substance in SCHEDULES II THROUGH V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) ePrescribing exception shall cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law. The s. 20(c) requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) does not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, although the immediate reduction to writing and the remaining validity duties still apply.
A shorter federal period controls where federal law requires one, such as the 7-day emergency oral Schedule II follow-up under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4).

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where state and federal law permit a WRITTEN prescription, 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to be issued on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and to be EITHER transmitted via facsimile or similar technology OR written on a TAMPER-RESISTANT FORM consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) states the same at statute level. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is INVALID AND SHALL NOT BE FILLED. An exception that permits a written prescription therefore removes the electronic-format mandate only; the written form requirements continue to govern the prescription the exception allows.
exceptions: The facsimile route and the tamper-resistant form route are alternatives; either satisfies 105 CMR 721.020(F)(1)-(2).

authority.name: Failover treated as an oral prescription

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.010 defines a FAILOVER as a document that ORIGINATES AS A SCHEDULE VI ELECTRONIC PRESCRIPTION, experiences an unforeseen defect during electronic transmission as outlined in Department guidance, and IS CONVERTED TO A COMPUTER GENERATED FACSIMILE. Only such a document qualifies. Under 105 CMR 721.020(G) a Failover SHALL BE CONSIDERED AN ORAL PRESCRIPTION and SHALL NOT REQUIRE a written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided all three conditions hold: it contains everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's signature and is immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or otherwise reduced to writing by the dispensing pharmacist; if the prescribing practitioner is not known to the dispensing pharmacist, that pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort to determine the Failover was issued by a prescribing practitioner; and the prescription is NOT FOR AN ADDITIONAL DRUG as defined in 105 CMR 700.001. Under 105 CMR 721.040(C) an electronic prescription transmitted by other means is invalid except in the event of a Failover verified under 721.020(G). A Schedule II through V oral prescription taken during a transmission outage is NOT a Failover; it falls under the separate 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) exception and still owes the 721.070(B) follow-up.
exceptions: A Failover is Schedule VI by definition; no Schedule II through V prescription can be one.
The three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G)(1)-(3) are conjunctive, and they apply only after the definitional test is met.
A Failover for an Additional Drug does not qualify, so the follow-up duty continues to apply to it.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) the information 105 CMR 700.012 requires shall be transmitted to the Department or its agent, in accordance with any procedures the Commissioner establishes, BY THE END OF THE NEXT BUSINESS DAY, and shall include data for ALL CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES DISPENSED SINCE THE PREVIOUS TRANSMISSION or report, by encrypted electronic device or electronic transmission method in a format the Commissioner approves. Under 700.012(A)(6) the Commissioner may waive that method for a pharmacy unable to submit electronically.
exceptions: The Commissioner may waive the electronic transmission method for a pharmacy unable to submit by electronic means.

full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Oral Prescriptions: Receipt, Follow-Up and Emergency Dispensing
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Receipt duties, follow-up documentation, Failover and emergency dispensing
learning_objectives: Carry out the pharmacist's duties at the moment an oral controlled-substance prescription is received.
Choose the follow-up period from the route the prescription travelled, and identify who owes it.
Separate the Schedule VI Failover from an ordinary electronic-prescribing outage.

quick_review.text: On receiving an oral controlled-substance prescription the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information Massachusetts requires, and must make a reasonable effort to authenticate a prescriber who is not known to the pharmacist.

The statutory default is an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days; the 7-day written route is available only where the practitioner has RECEIVED an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner, and that follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI.

Where the oral prescription for a Schedule II through V substance was issued under one of the enumerated electronic-prescribing exceptions, the regulation gives the practitioner not more than seven BUSINESS days and accepts either a written or an electronic prescription.

Most electronic-prescribing exceptions are categorical and are held by nobody: they attach to the prescription's circumstances, such as a veterinarian, a temporary technological failure, an emergency, or Schedule VI. Only a time-limited waiver is applied for and held.

A Failover is a Schedule VI device by definition: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, suffered a transmission defect, and was converted to a computer-generated facsimile. Only such a document counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up.

In an emergency a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II controlled substance on the practitioner's written or orally transmitted authorization, limited to the quantity adequate for the emergency period, with the practitioner owing a follow-up within seven business days.

decision_logic.condition: An oral controlled-substance prescription is received by telephone.
decision_logic.action: Reduce it to writing immediately with the required Massachusetts information, and authenticate the prescriber if that practitioner is not known to you.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber has not received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner.
decision_logic.action: Expect an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days; the 7-day written route is not open to that prescriber.

decision_logic.condition: The oral Schedule II through V prescription was issued under one of the enumerated electronic-prescribing exceptions.
decision_logic.action: Expect a written or electronic follow-up within not more than seven business days, and treat a shorter federal period as controlling where one applies.

decision_logic.condition: The document began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission, and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile.
decision_logic.action: Only then consider the Failover route, and only if all three of its conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug; otherwise the ordinary follow-up duty stands.

decision_logic.condition: A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission of a Schedule II through V prescription.
decision_logic.action: That is the ordinary outage exception, not a Failover. The prescription may be issued orally or in writing, and the follow-up duty remains.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist dispenses a Schedule II controlled substance on oral authorization in an emergency.
decision_logic.action: Limit the quantity to the emergency period, reduce the prescription to writing at once, authenticate an unknown prescriber, expect the follow-up within seven business days marked Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, attach it on receipt, and notify the DEA if it never comes.

ma_vs_federal.text: For an emergency oral Schedule II prescription Massachusetts measures the practitioner's follow-up in seven BUSINESS days while the federal rule allows seven days from the oral authorization, so the federal period is the shorter one and controls.

Both Massachusetts follow-up provisions carry the qualifier that a shorter federally required period controls, and the federal period they point at is the seven days for an emergency oral Schedule II follow-up.

exceptions.text: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, and the statutory follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI either.
A pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an exception or waiver.

The three Failover conditions sit downstream of the definition. Meeting all three does nothing for a prescription that was never a Schedule VI electronic prescription converted to a computer-generated facsimile.
An emergency waives only the electronic-prescribing requirement; every other prescription requirement continues to apply to the written or oral prescription the emergency permits.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner electronic follow-up after an oral controlled-substance prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the statutory default where the practitioner has received no electronic-prescribing exception.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner written follow-up where the practitioner has received a commissioner's exception
timing_deadlines.consequence: A mailed written prescription must be postmarked within the period.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner follow-up for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under an enumerated exception
timing_deadlines.consequence: Seven business days is a longer span than seven calendar days; either a written or an electronic prescription discharges it.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner follow-up after emergency oral Schedule II dispensing
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Seven business days under Massachusetts law, seven days under federal law
timing_deadlines.consequence: The federal seven days is shorter and controls; the document must bear Authorization for Emergency Dispensing.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing on a prescription form with the prescriber, patient, drug, directions, serial number and refill information Massachusetts requires.

The follow-up prescription must indicate on its face that it is issued to document an oral prescription, and on receipt the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it had reduced to writing; the pharmacist's record is incomplete until the two are joined.

A written follow-up must itself satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules: the practitioner's signature, and either transmission by facsimile or similar technology or a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements.
An emergency follow-up prescription bears Authorization for Emergency Dispensing on its face and is attached on receipt to the emergency prescription earlier reduced to writing.

role_duties.duty: Reduce the oral prescription to writing at once, authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber, join the follow-up document to it on arrival, and notify the DEA where an emergency follow-up never comes.
Deliver the follow-up prescription within the period that applies to the route the prescription travelled, in the form that route accepts.

common_traps.text: Calling any transmission outage a Failover waives a follow-up the law still requires; a Failover is Schedule VI by definition, and an outage affecting a Schedule II through V prescription is a different exception entirely.
Reading the three Failover conditions as the whole test misses the definitional limit sitting above them.
Treating every electronic-prescribing exception as something the prescriber holds misreads the list; most attach to the circumstances of the prescription and nobody applies for them.
Quoting seven days and seven business days as though they were the same period gets a follow-up delivered on day nine wrong in one direction or the other.
Looking only for a paper follow-up misses that the regulation accepts a written or an electronic prescription.
Applying the Massachusetts seven business days to an emergency oral Schedule II follow-up ignores the shorter federal seven days that controls it.
Accepting a follow-up on a form no permitted format supports leaves the file resting on an invalid prescription, which may not be filled at all.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 721.060(A) an Emergency Situation waives the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, so written and oral prescriptions may be issued, but they must comply with every other prescription requirement including 105 CMR 721.070(B). Under 721.060(B) a pharmacist may dispense a SCHEDULE II controlled substance on the written or orally transmitted authorization of a prescribing practitioner provided: the quantity is limited to the amount adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period; the prescription carries everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's actual signature and is immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or reduced to writing; if the practitioner is not known to the pharmacist, the pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort to determine the authorization came from a prescribing practitioner; WITHIN SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS the practitioner causes an electronic OR written prescription for the emergency quantity to be delivered, bearing 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' on its face, with a mailed written prescription postmarked within the period; and on receipt the pharmacist ATTACHES it to the orally transmitted prescription earlier reduced to writing. The pharmacist SHALL NOTIFY the nearest DEA office if the practitioner fails to deliver it.
exceptions: The emergency waiver removes the electronic-prescribing requirement only; every other prescription requirement, including 105 CMR 721.070(B), continues to apply.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The prescriber must deliver the required written or electronic follow-up Schedule II prescription to the pharmacy within seven days after authorizing emergency oral dispensing.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

full_prose_under_review.title: Prescriptions from Out-of-State Practitioners
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Presentation windows and the verification gate
learning_objectives: Choose the presentation window by the schedule of the substance, not by the federal refill clock.
Apply the mandatory verification gate before filling an out-of-state Schedule III through V prescription.
Separate the five-day window on the prescription from the five-day limit on an initial partial dispensing.
Carry out the post-fill reporting duty the Schedule II pathways impose.

quick_review.text: An authorized out-of-state practitioner's Schedule III through VI prescription may be filled in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding 30 days.
Massachusetts applies a five-day presentation window to out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions instead, under separate subsections with their own issuing-state conditions.
A Schedule III through V prescription on this pathway must be verified by the pharmacist, and may not be filled if verification cannot be obtained.
Where the out-of-state prescription is oral and in Schedules III through V, the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.
The Schedule II narcotic route reaches only a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth, and requires authentication and verification before the fill.

A prescription filled under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) has its own five-day limit on the INITIAL PARTIAL DISPENSING, which is a separate rule from the five-day window on when the prescription itself may be presented.
After filling an out-of-state Schedule II prescription the pharmacist must deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days, with the patient's name and address removed.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state practitioner's prescription is presented.
decision_logic.action: Identify the schedule first: Schedule III through VI runs on the 30-day window, Schedule II on the five-day window.

decision_logic.condition: The out-of-state prescription is in Schedules III through V.
decision_logic.action: Verify it by telephone or other means before filling, and do not fill it if verification cannot be obtained.

decision_logic.condition: The out-of-state Schedule III-V prescription was communicated orally.
decision_logic.action: Record that you requested the practitioner deliver or mail the written prescription within seven days or the shorter federal period.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state Schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) is partially dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Complete the initial partial dispensing not more than five days after the prescription issue date; the remaining portion still runs to 30 days after that issue date.

decision_logic.condition: You have filled an out-of-state Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the filling, excluding the patient's name and address.

ma_vs_federal.text: The federal six-month Schedule III-IV clock does not license an out-of-state prescription that Massachusetts no longer treats as fillable; the presentation window is the earlier gate.

exceptions.text: The five-day Schedule II window sits in separate subsections that also carry their own conditions on which issuing states qualify, so it is not simply a shorter version of the same rule.
Separate delivery provisions govern certain out-of-state residents, so the narcotic route is not simply the nonnarcotic route with a different list of states.

The out-of-state Schedule II subsections authorize the filling only. They do not authorize the practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances in the commonwealth or to practise here, and they do not authorize mail order pharmacies.

timing_deadlines.event: Out-of-state Schedule III through VI prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: Outside the window this pathway does not authorize the fill at all.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Presented within five days of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: The 30-day figure does not carry across to Schedule II.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner delivery of an out-of-state oral Schedule III-V written follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days or the shorter federal period
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period governs the practitioner's delivery or mailing, not the pharmacist's recording.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial partial dispensing of an out-of-state Schedule II prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 5 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: This limit governs the dispensing, while the separate five-day window governs when the prescription may be presented at all.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining portion of that partially dispensed prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remainder closes on the issue-date clock, not on the dispensing date.

timing_deadlines.event: Department copy after filling an out-of-state Schedule II prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This clock runs from the filling, unlike every other period in this section.

forms_records.text: On the out-of-state oral Schedule III-V pathway the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.
The Department copy excludes the patient's name and address, and neither the copy nor its contents is a public record.
An initial partial dispensing and any remainder on this pathway carry the s. 18(d3/4) patient-record notation of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed, accessible to the prescriber on request.

role_duties.duty: Verify an out-of-state Schedule III through V prescription before filling it, and refuse the fill where verification cannot be obtained.
Deliver the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of filling an out-of-state Schedule II prescription.

common_traps.text: Carrying the 30-day out-of-state window to a Schedule II prescription accepts one that Massachusetts allows only within five days of issue.
Filling an out-of-state Schedule III-V prescription on the federal six-month clock skips both the presentation window and the verification gate.
Treating the seven-day follow-up period as the pharmacist's deadline reverses the timed event.
Reading the five-day figure as one rule merges the window on presenting the prescription with the separate limit on completing an initial partial dispensing.
Measuring the Department copy's 30 days from the issue date rather than from the filling misses that this is the one duty here keyed to the dispensing event.

authority.name: Out-of-state Schedule III through VI prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription filled in Massachusetts within 30 days of issue; Schedule III through V prescriptions require pharmacist verification.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts applies a five-day presentation window and different issuing-state conditions to out-of-state narcotic and nonnarcotic Schedule II prescriptions.

authority.name: Massachusetts oral Schedule III through V follow-up request

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: For an oral Schedule III through V prescription issued under the out-of-state pathway, the pharmacist records requesting a written prescription within seven days or the shorter federal period.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts may fill a Schedule II narcotic prescription from Maine or a contiguous state within five days of issue after required authentication and verification; separate delivery provisions govern certain out-of-state residents.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4), read with s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription SHALL, if requested by the patient, dispense a lesser quantity; ONLY THE SAME PHARMACY that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion; a notation of the partial fill and quantity goes in the patient record, accessible to the prescriber on request; and the remaining portion MUST BE FILLED NOT LATER THAN 30 DAYS AFTER THE PRESCRIPTION ISSUE DATE. The separate FIVE-DAY limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing applies only to a prescription FILLED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (d) OR (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription issued by an out-of-state practitioner, and a narcotic Schedule II prescription issued by a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

authority.name: Out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II prescriptions, Department copy
Out-of-state narcotic Schedule II prescriptions, Department copy

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where a Schedule II prescription is filled under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) (a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner) or s. 18(d1/2) (a narcotic Schedule II prescription from a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth), the pharmacist SHALL, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER FILLING the prescription, DELIVER TO THE DEPARTMENT A COPY OF EACH SUCH SCHEDULE II PRESCRIPTION. The copy SHALL NOT INCLUDE THE NAME AND ADDRESS OF THE PATIENT for whom the prescription was issued, and neither the copy nor the information on it is a public record within M.G.L. c. 4, s. 7; both are subject to the restrictions in M.G.L. c. 66A, s. 2. Both subsections state this duty in the same terms. Neither subsection authorizes the out-of-state practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances under s. 9 or to practise within the commonwealth, and neither authorizes mail order pharmacies.
exceptions: The copy is anonymised: the patient's name and address are excluded.
The copy is not a public record and is subject to the M.G.L. c. 66A, s. 2 restrictions.
